report:
## Report

Your skepticism is well supported by the evidence. Controlled physiological studies consistently find that cloth and surgical masks do **not** cause dangerous CO2 buildup. A study of healthcare workers found CO2 concentrations rose modestly under masks but "remained below occupational safety thresholds" even with prolonged wear (Springer, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12879-021-06056-0). Direct measurement studies of N95 and surgical masks across activity levels similarly report increases that stay within safe limits (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11386028/). A randomized trial specifically testing prolonged N-95 mask use found **no significant CO2 retention or blood pH changes** in wearers (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8536290/). This is physiologically expected: CO2 molecules are far smaller than the pores in mask fabric and diffuse through easily, unlike larger respiratory droplets masks are designed to block.

The World Health Organization explicitly labels this claim a myth, stating that "the prolonged use of medical masks, when properly worn, does NOT cause CO2 intoxication nor oxygen deficiency," though masks may cause discomfort (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters). A USA Today fact-check reached the same conclusion, noting hypoxia/hypercapnia from ordinary mask wear is not supported by evidence (https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/05/30/fact-check-wearing-face-mask-not-cause-hypoxia-hypercapnia/5260106002/).

Some outlier papers (e.g., a "scoping review" cited in advocacy pieces) claim large CO2 elevations, but these are contested, not peer-reviewed clinical trials, and conflict with direct empirical measurements. Overall, the mainstream, experimentally verified conclusion is that the claim is false.
